v.why: With Adam each weight moves ~lr per step so the output change scales with fan-in, making wide nets diverge sooner when LR is raised.
Large batches give few updates per epoch and low-variance gradients, so bigger steps are both needed and safe.
Update effects compound across layers, so three-layer nets have a smaller stable LR range and suffer more from a step up.
sklearn applies L2 per minibatch, so larger batches mean fewer penalty applications per epoch, relieving over-shrinkage at high alpha.
Small batches at high LR combine large steps with high gradient variance, pushing training toward divergence.
Under a fixed 243-epoch budget a deeper net with tiny steps stays undertrained, so added depth cannot be exploited.
Narrow layers are a capacity bottleneck that an extra layer compensates for, whereas wide nets already have ample capacity.
Strong L2 shrinks every layer's weights, and stacking another shrunken layer compounds signal attenuation toward a constant predictor.
Wider layers change their outputs more per Adam step, partially offsetting the slow progress of tiny-LR training.
The L2 term sums over all weights, so widening under heavy alpha increases total shrinkage pressure and renders added units inert.

None of the remaining conditions switches off the edited component, so none is dropped for that reason.

Of the 17 left, I removed duplicates by mechanism:
- **Batch size and alpha:** both ideas rely on sklearn applying L2 per minibatch. I kept batch_size up conditioned on alpha high.
- **Depth and alpha:** both ideas are about shrinkage compounding across layers. I kept depth up conditioned on alpha high.
- **Batch size and learning rate:** I kept the high-LR divergence case. The tiny-LR undertraining case repeats the depth-and-low-LR idea.
- **Width and depth:** I kept depth up conditioned on width low.

That leaves 10 hypotheses, each with a different pair of parameters and a different mechanism. Most of them could plausibly go either way.
